lesson.title: Connecting the Dots: The Secant Line and What It Approximates
lesson.summary: A secant line joins two points on a curve and its slope is exactly the average rate of change between them, and watching that slope as the two points slide together previews how instantaneous rate of change is captured by a tangent line.
lesson.body:
A secant line is the straight line through any two distinct points on the graph of a function. Given points (a, f(a)) and (b, f(b)), the slope of the secant line connecting them is [f(b) - f(a)] divided by (b - a), which is precisely the average rate of change of f over the interval from a to b, and precisely the difference quotient evaluated with those two specific inputs. Graphing this line alongside the curve gives a direct visual meaning to average rate of change: it is literally the steepness of the chord cutting across the graph between the two chosen points.

Let f(x) = x^2 and draw the secant line through the points (1, 1) and (3, 9), since f(1) = 1 and f(3) = 9. The slope is (9 - 1)/(3 - 1) = 8/2 = 4. Using point-slope form with the point (1, 1): y - 1 = 4(x - 1), which simplifies to y = 4x - 3. Check this equation against both points: at x=1, y = 4(1) - 3 = 1, matching (1, 1); at x=3, y = 4(3) - 3 = 9, matching (3, 9). Both points lie on the line, confirming the secant line equation is correct, and its slope of 4 matches the average rate of change of x^2 over [1, 3] computed the same way average rate of change was defined earlier.

Now hold one endpoint fixed at x=1 and slide the other endpoint progressively closer to it. Through (1, 1) and (1.5, 2.25): slope = (2.25 - 1)/(1.5 - 1) = 1.25/0.5 = 2.5. Through (1, 1) and (1.1, 1.21): slope = (1.21 - 1)/(1.1 - 1) = 0.21/0.1 = 2.1. Through (1, 1) and (1.01, 1.0201): slope = (1.0201 - 1)/(1.01 - 1) = 0.0201/0.01 = 2.01. As the second point slides toward (1, 1), the secant slope drifts from 4 down through 2.5, 2.1, and 2.01, closing in on 2.

Approaching from the other side tells the same story. Through (1, 1) and (0.5, 0.25): slope = (0.25 - 1)/(0.5 - 1) = (-0.75)/(-0.5) = 1.5. Through (1, 1) and (0.9, 0.81): slope = (0.81 - 1)/(0.9 - 1) = (-0.19)/(-0.1) = 1.9. Through (1, 1) and (0.99, 0.9801): slope = (0.9801 - 1)/(0.99 - 1) = (-0.0199)/(-0.01) = 1.99. Sliding the second point toward x=1 from below produces the same limiting slope of 2 that was found sliding in from above, so the secant slope converges to a single instantaneous rate of change regardless of which side the second point approaches from, unlike the one-sided infinite limits seen earlier where left and right behavior could disagree.

That limiting value, 2, is exactly the instantaneous rate of change of f(x) = x^2 at x=1, which matches the difference quotient pattern 2x + h found for x^2, evaluated at x=1 and taken to its limit as h approaches 0. This is the deeper reason secant lines matter: as the second point is pulled toward the first, the secant line pivots and approaches a limiting position called the tangent line, whose slope is the instantaneous rate of change at that single point. Graphing several secant lines through a fixed point, each with the second point closer than the last, makes this convergence visible directly on the graph rather than only in a table of numbers.

Every idea in this cluster fits together through the secant line: average rate of change is secant slope, the difference quotient is secant slope written algebraically with a variable step h, and instantaneous rate of change is the limiting slope those secant lines approach as the step shrinks to zero, which is the slope of the tangent line at that point.
